title: HRV-Based Training for Improving VO2max in Endurance Athletes. A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis
authors: Granero-Gallegos A, González-Quílez A, Plews D, Carrasco-Poyatos M
journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
population: Trained endurance athletes in RCTs of HRV-guided vs control training with a VO2max outcome
findings: Only randomised controlled trials in trained athletes with a VO2max outcome were included; random-effects meta-analysis with moderator analyses (athlete level and sex) and meta-regression by group size.
Both HRV-guided and control training improved VO2max (p < 0.0001), but the effect size for HRV-guided training was significantly higher (p < 0.0001; ES HRVG-CG = 0.187).
The amateur-level and female subgroups showed better and significant VO2max results (p < 0.0001).
HRV-guided training had a small (ES = 0.402) but positive effect on VO2max, conditioned by athlete level and sex.
limitations: Number of RCTs and participants not in the abstract; VO2max only, not race performance; subgroup findings are moderator analyses, not randomised comparisons; the abstract reports 0.187 and 0.402 without clarifying which comparison each describes.
implications: The benefit signal is larger in amateur athletes and women, which supports default-on HRV adjustment for recreational users; sex-specific evidence is subgroup-driven and thin.
Keep HRV rules conservative and treat any VO2max benefit as small (ES about 0.2 to 0.4).
Store sex and training level as inputs, but do not hard-code sex-specific HRV thresholds on this evidence.

verification.notes: Crossref confirms title, journal, first author, 30 Oct 2020. p-values and ES verified in the raw Europe PMC abstract (PMID 33143175).
